_readme: Per guide → per step index (1-based): type frame|clip|audio, at = seconds into the FINAL, caption = what to look at and why this step caused it. Hand-picked from contact sheets in .temp/evidence/sheets/.

1.caption: Her forearm crops the bottom of the frame and the lens is a hand's length from her face — that is the whole format, before a single beat happens.

2.caption: She looks at the shaker, stretches her arms overhead, leans back in to talk. Four seconds of nothing happening — that is the beat list working.

1.caption: Round image, hard black corners — even a steel steam tray of tteokbokki bows at the edges. Crop this to 16:9 and it is ordinary food stock footage.

2.caption: The cup is handed across the counter, then she is eating under the bulb. Showing the hand-off is why the cup can never appear out of nowhere later.

1.caption: The lens is on the ground: the sneaker is the nearest thing in frame, the brick and the roller shutters bend away into the black corners. Same street at eye level would be unremarkable.

2.caption: Four seconds, four shots — two from directly overhead, the headphone macro, then straight back down to pavement level. Nothing is held long enough to explain itself.

1.caption: The middle of the ad, with no product in it at all: the tail of the vortex, a cream-white wave, then water hitting hair. Moving water is the only thing holding these cuts together.

2.caption: Read the label: the brand line holds, the sub-line under it came out as "ANTI ING ECALR". Large type survives, small type does not.

1.caption: Every rail row carries two lines — Liver, then Digestive System under it. The list groups the body before a single organ is opened.

2.caption: The eye's facts read Size, Weight, Daily, Location, Blood supply, Function. The liver's list is different — same panel, different keys.

1.caption: Same rifle, same snow, three shots apart — the weapon and weather were locked before any route was written.

2.caption: Tunnel into corridor in one continuous pass. Rooms chain; there is no cut to hide behind.

1.caption: Caramel → pour → whisk: the shot list is literally the recipe order.

2.caption: The character appears only in the last second. Everything before is hands and food.

1.caption: Edges are ragged on purpose — the scan was framed so the splat falls apart where nobody looks.

2.caption: The camera orbits the fridge and drifts to the booth. No fly-through, no vertical move — that is what keeps the splat solid.

1.caption: The library grid. Categories on the left are the taxonomy from the brief — the agent filed every render into one.

2.caption: One scene, one technique: rain on a puddle, nothing else in frame. Each tile in the library is this focused.

1.caption: Genshin → God of War skin swap. Watch the silhouette — one mesh, only the material changes.

2.caption: The skin rail on the right is the only control on the page. Everything else reacts to it.

1.caption: The handheld wobble on entry. The camera operator is a character — that came from the prompt, not post.

2.caption: The one human beat: she turns to the lens after a win. The timeline was built around this second.

1.caption: Hero, palette and ink outline fixed in frame one. Every later shot inherits exactly this.

2.caption: Market rooftops into the castle wall. The chase is a route with a destination, not a loop.

1.caption: Desert into water. Two of the four biomes, recognisable before the transition finishes.

2.caption: Cubic lily pads, photoreal water. Geometry stays blocky; light, texture and volume do not.

1.caption: Mid-burst and the rifle has not changed shape since the first frame. "Prop bolted to the camera" did that.

2.caption: Classroom into stairwell. One direction of travel, one turn — the room-by-room route from step 2.

1.caption: Same living room, same brief, two models side by side. Differences you see are the models', not the prompt's.

2.caption: The kitchen pass on both. Neither take was regenerated — this is the first output each model returned.

1.caption: Health bars, timer, round counter — all rendered as part of the image, not overlaid.

2.caption: The first two of six choreographed hits. Each has a wind-up and a landing you can count.

1.caption: Rain and mist lead the frame; the operator is secondary. Weather was written first in the prompt.

2.caption: Open treeline into the cabin doorway. The space closes in — the only structural move in the piece.

1.caption: The heroine block: cloak, hair, silhouette. Pasted verbatim into every shot so she never drifts.

2.caption: Lake to courtyard. Environments change on the six-second beat; she does not.

1.caption: Available light, over-the-shoulder, nobody posed. "Documentary, not cinema" is the difference.

2.caption: Four seconds of the single continuous walk. There is no second shot to cut to.

1.caption: The starting state before any edit — this is what the audit was run against.

3.caption: Canvas grain on the cards and the retuned key light. Compare with the frame under step 1.

4.caption: Cards cycling with the new English copy and Quadcode-guide roles.

1.caption: Rail, landing, roll-out in one line. Nothing here is a cut between separate tricks.

2.caption: Mid-flip and the feet still read as over the board. This is the contact rule holding.

3.caption: The HUD scores the trick as it lands. It confirms the move instead of decorating the frame.

4.caption: The roll-away. The cut lands here, not on the landing — the trick gets to finish.

1.caption: Minimap, health, mission marker — framed exactly like a capture, which is why it reads as gameplay.

2.caption: One wave, one readable line from lip to trough. No secondary swell to confuse the eye.

3.caption: HUD state after the move: the score and marker changed with it.

4.caption: Tail of the single continuous take that was kept. Other takes were dropped, not stitched.

1.caption: The one rule: motion leaves ink. Everything in the piece obeys it.

2.caption: The sword arc drawing the stroke in real time. The graphic is a by-product of the movement.

3.caption: The payoff: strokes resolve into the dragon. One image, not a montage.

4.caption: Final seconds. The dragon holds without drift — the retake this step describes.

1.caption: The boss silhouette in full. Read it against the trees — it is not borrowed from any franchise.

2.caption: Blocking: the boss approaches, camera holds, hero enters. Directed as a scene, not a slideshow.

3.caption: The impact signature — one golden arc. Every hit in the piece uses this and only this.

1.caption: Dial macro, before and after. The model matched to this footage keeps engraving crisp without inventing texture.

2.caption: Beach shot. Grain is still there after the upscale — the conservative noise setting from this step.

1.caption: The product exists from frame one. The single-line invention is the whole brief.

2.caption: The ironing pass with captions riding along. Both were directed in the same prompt.

3.caption: The cleanest pass: crumpled to flat with no seam artefacts. This is the take that was kept.

1.caption: Both models, first frame, same brief. Any difference from here on is the model's decision.

2.caption: The same beat on each model, side by side. One take each, no reroll.

1.caption: The macro opener: needle in the yolk. Scale is established before anything moves.

2.caption: The detonation. It is one continuous transformation, not a cut to an after-state.

1.caption: Beat one of three: surface, ship, king. The script gave both models the same three beats.

2.caption: Beat two underwater on both models. Same words, visibly different readings.

1.caption: A crowd holding phones, a pier, midday sun. The staging says "someone filmed this", not "a studio lit this".

2.caption: The impossible step off the pier. The camera keeps its phone-footage wobble through it.

1.caption: The laptop is a real object in a real scene before anything breaks out of it.

2.caption: The breakout. The parrot leaves the screen and lands on a hand — one move, no cut.

1.caption: The hero keyframe — label dead-on, petals frozen. The loop was built out from this single frame.

2.caption: Rotation with a slow push-in. The loop returns to the keyframe without a visible join.

1.caption: Hero section typing in: serif, sakura pink, one product shot. The mood was set here before any layout.

2.caption: Scrolling the structure — collection, hero product, philosophy. The order came from step 2.

1.caption: Fisheye vignette, DV colour, burned-in date. The camera was specified, not the style.

2.caption: The one small moment: a stray cat, a hand held out. Nothing else happens, and nothing else needs to.

3.caption: The glance back. This is the honest take — the one that was kept over prettier, stiffer ones.

1.caption: The pipeline: actor → prompt → product → output. The actor tile is the same in every frame.

2.caption: Bag in hand, consistent with the product tile. The compositing step is what puts it there.

3.caption: The output panel in motion. Same actor, same bag, now video.

1.caption: The shell as a dot field. Still a photo — every dot samples one pixel.

2.caption: Cursor moves across, dots scatter and settle. The reaction is what step 2 wired in.

1.caption: Intro. The room tone — brushed drums, low keys — is the "vibe" line from the prompt, verbatim.

2.caption: Guitar and Rhodes enter. Naming instruments is why these two are here and nothing else is.

3.caption: The finish. Tempo holds to the end and the track resolves instead of fading.

4.caption: The hook from the take that was kept. Compare against your own generations at the same point.

1.caption: Opening bars. Genre and instrumentation are audible in the first four.

2.caption: The 30-second turn — an edit point written into the prompt as ad structure.

4.caption: The cleanest take, final third. No stray artefacts on the sustained notes.

1.caption: The groove locks in immediately. Instrumentation was named, not described.

2.caption: Brass stabs land on the grid — each one is a place a cut can sit.

4.caption: The punchiest take, final third. Transients are sharp all the way through.

1.caption: Deliberately sparse from bar one. Space is the brief.

2.caption: Midsection. Nothing sits in the voice range — the room left for a voiceover.

4.caption: The take with the most space, final third. Fewest elements, longest gaps.
